CHAPTER 01 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Your next chapter starts at sea.

Mariela, your experience is the story. You do not need to become someone else on camera. You need a clear promise, a little preparation, and room for your warmth to shine.

BEFORE YOU START · MAKE FILMING EASIER TO MANAGE

Give your content a little space of its own.

Mariela, creating content means recording several versions of a sentence, extra views of the ship, and clips you may never use. That adds up quickly. Since you cruise so often, look into a dedicated second phone or a DJI Osmo Pocket 3 Creator Combo (the creator bundle) so your personal phone is not doing every job or filling up with every recording.

You can still practice with your current phone. A separate device becomes useful when storage, battery life, or finding clips starts making the process harder.

Option 1 · A second phone for content

What it is: A separate phone used mainly for recording, editing, and organizing cruise videos. An older phone you already own may be enough.

Why consider it: Familiar controls, a larger screen for reading and editing, and a separate camera roll. Your everyday phone stays available for messages, travel information, and personal photos.

Before choosing: Check usable storage, battery health, microphone compatibility, and whether your editing apps run well. A separate cellular plan is usually unnecessary for basic recording and editing; uploads still need an internet connection.

Good fit if: You want a familiar, all-in-one filming and editing device with fewer new controls to learn.

Option 2 · DJI Osmo Pocket 3 Creator Combo

What it is: A compact handheld camera with a gimbal—a motorized support that helps keep the picture steady as you move. The Creator Combo bundles creator accessories; check the exact contents offered where you buy.

Why consider it: It gives filming its own device, with mechanical stabilization for gentle walking shots and a screen you can turn for different recording orientations.

Storage matters: Pocket 3 has no built-in storage; it records to a compatible microSD card. A microSD card is a small removable memory card. Budget for a card from DJI’s current recommended list and a way to copy files to your editing device.

Good fit if: You want a separate camera for frequent filming and are comfortable learning how to record, use audio accessories, transfer footage, and charge another device.

Separate filming does not automatically solve storage.

If you copy every camera clip onto your personal phone to edit, that phone can still fill up. Choose where your originals, editing files, and finished videos will live before your next sailing. A computer or dedicated editing phone can help; cloud backups depend on a usable connection and may involve storage fees.

  1. Record in small pieces: one thought per clip, plus the few extra views you need. Stop recording between useful moments.
  2. Sort each evening: put useful clips in a folder named by sailing and topic. Mark favorites so you can find them later.
  3. Copy and back up: keep two copies of important footage in separate places. Open a few copied files to confirm they play before removing originals from a device or card.
  4. Edit a selection: transfer the clips you actually need rather than the whole trip. Keep an organized archive of the rest.
  5. Practice before departure: record, play back with sound, transfer, edit, and export one complete test video at home.
A sensible first step: Try a spare phone if you have one. If you are ready for a separate camera, compare the Pocket 3 Creator Combo’s current price, included accessories, and learning effort with a dedicated phone. Choose the setup you can comfortably carry and use—not simply the one with the most features.

Equipment details checked November 2, 2026. See DJI’s Pocket 3 overview, specifications and storage details, and support and transfer guidance. Prices, bundles, availability, and compatibility can change. This equipment suggestion is not a DJI sponsorship or affiliate offer.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Start here: what content creation actually means

Content, posts, and platforms

What it is: Content is something you make to share an idea: a video, photo, written answer, or live conversation. A post is one published piece. A platform is the service where people see it, such as Instagram or YouTube.

Why it matters: A helpful video does not have to be a big production. You can start with one clear answer and the phone you already have.

Cruise example: A 25-second video showing what you keep in your embarkation-day bag is one piece of content.

Your first try: Choose one platform you already use comfortably and make one short, useful video for it.

Audience and value

What it is: Your audience is the person or group you hope to help. Value is what they gain: an answer, a useful idea, reassurance, or enjoyment.

Why it matters: Knowing who you are speaking to helps you decide what to explain and what to leave out.

Cruise example: A first-time cruiser needs to know what embarkation means; someone who cruises every month may want a specific cabin comparison.

Your first try: Finish this sentence before recording: “This video helps [person] understand [one thing].”

Your personal brand

What it is: Your brand is the recognizable promise, personality, and style people come to expect from you. It includes your name and design, but also how honestly and warmly you explain things.

Why it matters: A consistent identity helps viewers remember you and understand why they should return.

Cruise example: “Loyal to Royal” can mean Mariela’s warm, experienced perspective on Royal Caribbean, with honest explanations of costs and limits.

Your first try: Introduce yourself in your own voice. You do not need to sound like an advertisement.

The creation process

What it is: Most content follows five stages: plan the idea, record it, edit it, publish it, and learn from the response. Editing means choosing and arranging what you recorded.

Why it matters: Breaking the work into small stages makes it less overwhelming and prevents filming without knowing the point.

Cruise example: Choose a carry-on tip → record yourself and the bag → trim pauses → add captions → publish → note the questions people ask.

Your first try: Read the hook, camera, sound, and editing lessons before your first practice video. Save brand reporting and advanced metrics for later.

Your beginner route: For your first video, learn one hook, record one sentence at eye level, add one detail shot, and correct the captions. On your next video, improve one more thing. You do not need to master the entire playbook at once.

Now put it into practice

Your point of view

A retired cruiser who sails about monthly, loves Royal Caribbean, and explores without flying. Help people picture a vacation they can actually take.

Your audience

Start with first-time cruisers, travelers who prefer driving to a port, retirees, and repeat guests trying to understand value. Address one person and one question per video.

Your promise

“I’m Mariela Alvarez. I cruise often, and I’ll show you what I actually use, what costs extra, and what I’d do differently.” Keep your own natural phrasing.

Loyal to Royal. Honest with you. A personal creator identity inspired by Mariela’s enthusiasm. This playbook is independent and is not an official Royal Caribbean publication. A hosted trip never requires a glowing review.

The first week: small wins

A repeatable content mix

For every ten posts, try four useful answers, two personal stories, two ship or port walkthroughs, one value comparison, and one community reply. Sponsored work can fit these formats; disclose the relationship in each relevant post. Adjust this mix using your results, not a rigid quota.

“I don’t fly, but I’m still seeing the world—one sailing at a time.”A possible opening line, if it feels true to you.

CHAPTER 02 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Earn the first few seconds.

Learn what a hook is, how a content angle differs from a camera angle, and why each helps your story.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Hooks and angles: two different choices

A hook

What it is: A hook is the opening sentence, image, or action that gives someone a reason to keep watching. It usually appears in the first few seconds.

Why it matters: People scrolling do not yet know why your video is useful. A clear hook tells them what question you will answer.

Cruise example: Instead of “Hi everyone, I’m on a cruise again,” try “Before you check your suitcase, keep these three things with you.” Show the bag as you speak.

Your first try: Write the viewer’s question first. Turn your answer into one short opening sentence, and make sure the video delivers it.

A content angle

What it is: A content angle is the specific point of view you choose for a topic. It answers, “Which part of this subject am I explaining, and for whom?” It does not describe where you hold the camera.

Why it matters: A broad topic can become too much for one video. One angle makes the story focused and easier to follow.

Cruise example: Topic: cruise cabins. Possible angles: storage for a long trip, cabin location for a light sleeper, or choosing a cabin when you want fewer stairs.

Your first try: Choose one topic and finish: “I’m looking at this through the needs of [viewer].” Use that angle to decide which details belong.

A camera angle

What it is: A camera angle is the position and direction of the camera relative to its subject: eye level, looking down, or looking up.

Why it matters: Camera position changes what viewers can see and how a shot feels. It is a filming choice, separate from your story’s angle.

Cruise example: Your content angle is carry-on essentials for beginners. You speak at eye level, then film downward into your open bag.

Your first try: Start with eye level when speaking. Use a downward view only when it helps show an object or action.

Storytelling and a story arc

What it is: Storytelling connects events so the viewer understands what happened and why it mattered. A story arc is its path: a situation, a question or difficulty, an experience, and a takeaway.

Why it matters: A list tells people facts; a story helps them understand and remember how those facts apply.

Cruise example: “I used to pack everything in my suitcase. Then I needed something before my room was ready. Now these essentials stay in my carry-on.”

Your first try: Tell one true moment in four sentences: what I expected, what happened, what I did, and what I learned.

A call to action, or CTA

What it is: A call to action is the one next step you invite a viewer to take after receiving the useful information.

Why it matters: A specific invitation gives the video a helpful ending and makes it easier for viewers to respond.

Cruise example: “Save this list for packing day” fits a packing video. “Which cabin question should I answer next?” invites useful comments.

Your first try: Choose one natural next step. You do not need to ask for likes, follows, shares, and bookings all at once.

See the whole chain: Topic: cabins → content angle: storage for first-time cruisers → hook: “This is the cabin storage I nearly missed” → proof: open the drawer → camera angle: a close downward view → CTA: “Save this before you unpack.” The subject, viewpoint, opening, evidence, filming position, and invitation each have a different job.

Now put it into practice

A simple 30-second structure

  1. 0–3 seconds: show the result or ask the actual question.
  2. 3–8: explain who this helps and identify ship/sailing if relevant.
  3. 8–23: demonstrate two or three useful steps.
  4. 23–28: explain the limitation or tradeoff.
  5. 28–30: offer one useful next action.

These are practice timings, not platform rules. Deliver a sponsored disclosure at the start with the endorsement; never postpone it to protect the hook.

Show, then explain

Open on the drawer that fits your packing cubes, the quiet seat, or the lunch you chose. Start the sentence over that image. Skip a long greeting, animated logo, and “wait until the end.”

Story arc: I expected → I noticed → I tried → here’s what I’d do next time. Include one honest inconvenience. That is often the most useful part.

Hook library: borrow the structure

Make a stronger promise

Vague: “Cruising is amazing!” → Useful: “Three things I keep in my carry-on before my cabin is ready.”
Overclaim: “Everyone gets free drinks!” → Accurate: “Here’s the drink benefit listed for my loyalty tier—and what you should verify.”

Pick a single call to action: “Save this for embarkation day,” “Which cabin question should I answer next?” or “Check your sailing’s app for the current details.” Avoid stacking requests to like, follow, share, comment, and book.

CHAPTER 03 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Make the camera feel like a friend.

Learn how to position your phone, choose what appears in the picture, and speak to the person behind the lens.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Understand what the camera is doing

A shot, a clip, and a take

What it is: A shot is a particular view of your subject. A clip is a recorded video segment. A take is one attempt at recording a moment or sentence.

Why it matters: You can make a video from several short clips. You do not have to deliver a perfect speech in one take.

Cruise example: Record one take explaining the drawer, then a separate clip of opening it.

Your first try: Record one sentence twice. Pick whichever version sounds most like you.

Framing and composition

What it is: Framing is what you include inside the picture and what you leave outside it. Composition is how you arrange people, objects, and empty space within that frame.

Why it matters: Viewers should immediately see what matters. A cluttered background or a cut-off face can distract from your explanation.

Cruise example: For a talking video, include your head and upper chest. For a packing demonstration, include the bag and both hands.

Your first try: Before recording, look at all four edges of the screen. Remove distractions and check that the important object is fully visible.

Placement, headroom, and safe areas

What it is: Placement means where your face, objects, and text sit on screen. Headroom is the space above your head. A safe area is space that stays clear of a platform’s buttons and labels.

Why it matters: Poor placement can put captions over your mouth or hide a price behind an app button.

Cruise example: Place yourself a little to one side when a list needs room beside you. Keep important text away from the bottom and right edges.

Your first try: Record a short test, then preview it in the posting screen. Move anything that the app controls cover.

Eyeline and the lens

What it is: Your eyeline is where your eyes appear to be looking. The lens is the small camera opening, not the image of your face on the screen.

Why it matters: Looking at the lens feels like eye contact with the viewer. Reading from a screen to the side makes your gaze drift away from them.

Cruise example: If your script sits next to the phone, viewers see you looking sideways. Three cue words beside the lens reduce that movement.

Your first try: Find the lens. Look at it and say one sentence as if speaking to a friend. Watch it back and compare it with a sentence read from the side.

A script, cue words, and a teleprompter

What it is: A script is the wording you plan to say. Cue words remind you of ideas without writing every word. A teleprompter displays your script near the camera so you can read while speaking.

Why it matters: Preparation helps you stay on topic, but trying to read too much can make delivery stiff and your eyes visibly scan.

Cruise example: For a bag video, your cues might be “room not ready / essentials / check timing.” Explain each thought naturally.

Your first try: Start with cue words and one sentence per take. Try a teleprompter only if you still need the full script.

Aspect ratio, resolution, frame rate, focus, and exposure

What it is: Aspect ratio is the picture’s shape: 9:16 is tall and narrow. Resolution describes picture detail; 1080p is a common setting. Frame rate counts pictures per second; 30 fps is a common starting setting. Focus controls sharpness. Exposure controls brightness.

Why it matters: Basic settings help your footage look consistent and keep your face clear. A bright ocean can otherwise leave your face too dark.

Cruise example: A vertical 1080p, 30 fps clip can be a simple starting point for a short video. Tap your face to focus and check its brightness.

Your first try: Use a single simple setup first. Record and review a ten-second test before filming a whole explanation.

Now put it into practice

◯
╱│╲
EYES NEAR UPPER THIRDKeep captions
clear of your face.LEAVE SPACE FOR APP CONTROLS

The everyday phone setup

  1. Wipe the lens. Put the phone on a stable support at eye height.
  2. Start with vertical 9:16 for short video. Use 1080p at 30 fps as a simple default; choose higher resolution only if storage and editing can support it.
  3. Use the rear camera when someone can frame you; the front camera is fine for solo practice. Check the actual lens position.
  4. Stand about an arm’s length away, with a little room above your head and eyes near the upper third.
  5. Put your face slightly off-center if text or a demonstration needs space. Keep the horizon straight.
  6. Lock focus/exposure if your phone supports it. Lower exposure a little if sea or sky turns white.

Keep essential text away from the bottom, right edge, and top controls. A starting margin is about 15% at top/bottom and 10% at sides; platform overlays vary. Preview the actual upload before posting.

Stop looking off-screen to read

Use three cue words

Write “problem / proof / takeaway” directly beside the lens. Explain the idea to one imagined friend. Use short takes of one thought each.

Try record → pause → repeat

Read the next line, look up, breathe, then deliver it. Trim the reading and pauses later. Cover edits with the thing you are describing.

If you use a teleprompter

Place text close to the lens, use large type and narrow lines, and slow the scroll to your voice. Move the phone farther back if your eyes visibly scan. Practice without scrolling first.

Choose a useful camera view

ShotUse it forHow to capture
Eye-level mediumTrust and explanationChest-up, steady phone, quiet backdrop
Wide establishingWhere are we?Venue or ship view; avoid identifiable guests
Close detailProofMenu price, storage latch, food texture; hide private data
Over shoulder / point of viewHow it worksDemonstrate on your own device or belongings
Gentle walk-throughLayout and routeMove slowly, elbows tucked; stop before speaking
Low or high accentVarietyA brief ship exterior or overhead packing shot; no unsafe reach
The five-shot recipe: one wide view, one medium view, two close details, one reaction. Hold each for 5–8 seconds so the editor has choices. Record a second clean take of anything essential. Never lean beyond a railing or block a walkway for a shot.

CHAPTER 04 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Beautiful light. Understandable words.

A simple setup that you can repeat on every cruise.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Light and audio make the message easy to receive

Lighting and backlighting

What it is: Lighting is how light falls on your subject. Backlighting happens when a bright source is behind you, such as a sunny window.

Why it matters: The camera may expose for the bright background and leave your face in shadow. Viewers need to see your expression and the item you are demonstrating.

Cruise example: In your cabin, face the window rather than standing with it behind you.

Your first try: Turn toward a window and record a test. Compare it with a test facing away from the window.

Audio and microphone distance

What it is: Audio is the sound in your video: speech, surroundings, and music. A microphone picks it up; a lavalier is a small microphone clipped near your mouth.

Why it matters: If speech is distant, windy, or muffled, viewers have to work to understand you. Clear sound makes your explanation easier to follow.

Cruise example: The pool deck looks lovely, but wind and music may drown out your words. A quiet cabin can be better for the explanation.

Your first try: Try your phone’s microphone in a quiet spot first. Listen to a test before deciding whether you need another microphone.

Voiceover, natural sound, and music

What it is: A voiceover is narration recorded separately and played over pictures. Natural sound is the sound of the place or action. Background music adds mood under the main audio.

Why it matters: These layers do different jobs. A voiceover lets you explain noisy footage clearly; excessive music can hide the explanation.

Cruise example: Show the drawer opening while a separately recorded voice says, “This is where I kept my folded shirts.”

Your first try: Record one silent detail clip and explain it afterward in a quiet room. You can leave music out of your first video.

Sound levels and a windscreen

What it is: Sound level is how loud a recording or audio layer is. A windscreen is a foam or furry cover that helps reduce wind noise on a microphone.

Why it matters: Very loud sound can distort, while low speech becomes hard to hear. Wind can overwhelm a microphone even when you are close to it.

Cruise example: A necklace can rub against a clip-on microphone and create scratching sounds.

Your first try: Make a short recording wearing your filming clothes. Listen for rubbing, wind, and words that disappear.

Now put it into practice

Light your face

Face a window or open shade. Keep strong sun behind the phone, not behind you. Turn off a harsh overhead light if it creates deep eye shadows. Avoid mixing orange cabin light and blue window light.

Choose a quieter corner

Step away from pool music, public-address speakers, engines, and wind. Record a 10-second test and listen with headphones. If words are unclear, change location before changing equipment.

Use a close microphone

A small lavalier with a windscreen can help. Keep it away from jewelry, scarves, and rubbing fabric. Check battery, connection, and levels. Record a backup voice note when a take matters.

The carry-on creator kit

Phone, charging cable, permitted power bank, compact phone grip or tripod, headphones, optional lavalier and windscreen, lens cloth, and a small pouch. Check current prohibited-item and battery rules before packing. Do not attach gear to ship fixtures without permission.

When the ship is loud

Film silent supporting footage, then record narration in your cabin. Say what the viewer is seeing: “This drawer fit my folded shirts.” Capture a few seconds of natural sound when permitted, and keep background music below speech. Use licensed music cleared for your platform and commercial use; a popular sound is not automatically cleared for sponsored content or brand ads.

A two-minute preflight

CHAPTER 05 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Edit for clarity, then personality.

One useful idea, a visible example, and no extra work for the viewer.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Editing is choosing what helps the viewer

Editing, trimming, and cuts

What it is: Editing means selecting and arranging clips and sound into a finished video. Trimming shortens a clip. A cut is the change from one clip to another.

Why it matters: You can remove the moments spent looking at your notes and keep the useful explanation. The viewer only needs the finished idea.

Cruise example: Record “Here is what I pack,” pause to check your notes, and record the next thought. Remove the pause between those thoughts.

Your first try: Make a video from two short clips. Trim only the extra time before and after each sentence.

A-roll, B-roll, and a jump cut

What it is: A-roll is your main explanation, often you speaking to the camera. B-roll is supporting footage that shows what you are discussing. A jump cut is a noticeable skip between two moments in a similar view.

Why it matters: Supporting footage gives the viewer proof and can cover an edit between sentences so the change feels natural.

Cruise example: A-roll: you explain cabin storage. B-roll: the drawer opening. Lay the drawer footage over your explanation while your voice continues.

Your first try: Record one talking clip and one close-up of the thing you mention. Use the close-up during the matching sentence.

Pacing

What it is: Pacing is how quickly your video moves through information, pictures, and pauses. It is the rhythm of the experience.

Why it matters: Dragging out an obvious point can lose attention; rushing a demonstration can make it impossible to follow.

Cruise example: Show a storage latch long enough for someone to see how it opens. Cut a long walk down a corridor if it adds no information.

Your first try: Watch your draft and ask, “Does the viewer need more time here, or have I already made the point?”

Captions, subtitles, and the post caption

What it is: On-screen captions are written versions of speech displayed during the video; they can also identify meaningful sounds. Subtitles often refer to dialogue text or translation. The post caption is the description written below the video.

Why it matters: On-screen captions help people watching without sound and people who need text access. The description below the post does not replace them.

Cruise example: Video text says “Keep essentials with you” as you speak. The post caption adds the ship, date, and source details.

Your first try: Use automatic captions if available, then correct every word and check that the text stays readable.

Transitions, covers, and exports

What it is: A transition is how one shot changes to the next; a simple cut is enough. A cover or thumbnail is the image representing a video before it plays. Exporting saves the edited video as a shareable file.

Why it matters: Clear covers help people find the right video. A clean export gives you a finished copy to keep or upload. Fancy transitions are optional.

Cruise example: A simple cover reading “MY CARRY-ON LIST” tells viewers what the video covers. Save a final copy after checking captions and sound.

Your first try: Use simple cuts and a readable cover. Keep your original clips and a finished copy in separate folders.

Now put it into practice

A practical editing pass

  1. Build the spine. Choose the clearest opening and your best explanation. Cut the setup before the point.
  2. Remove friction. Trim long hesitations and repeated sentences. Keep natural breaths and warmth.
  3. Add proof. Place supporting footage over the exact sentence it illustrates. Don’t cover every second with unrelated scenery.
  4. Change with purpose. Try a visual change every 2–4 seconds in a short tip, then let a detailed demonstration breathe. Avoid frantic zooms and flashing cuts.
  5. Balance sound. Make speech consistent and music quiet. Listen through both headphones and the phone speaker.
  6. Caption, fact-check, export. Watch once with sound off and once with your eyes off the screen. Each should still make sense.

Captions are part of the video

Readable

Use large, high-contrast text with a solid or shaded backing. Limit to one or two lines and split at natural phrases. Keep captions inside the upload’s safe area.

Accurate

Generate automatic captions, then correct every line: Mariela, ship names, CocoCay, Crown & Anchor, prices, and numbers. Match what is said; don’t quietly change the claim in text.

Accessible

Add native closed captions where supported as well as readable on-screen captions when useful. Describe important visual details in the narration. Don’t communicate meaning through color alone.

Sample 35-second cut

TimePictureAudio / text
0–4Mariela + carry-on“Your cabin may not be ready. Here’s what stays with me.” Add sponsorship disclosure if relevant.
4–12Close details of bagMedication, required documents, charging cable—show your own items without sensitive labels.

Keep a clean exported master without a platform watermark. Give each post a cover with 3–6 useful words, such as “FIRST HOUR ONBOARD.” Export a vertical MP4 compatible with your platform; check its current upload settings rather than assuming one duration or file limit fits everywhere.

CHAPTER 06 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

A whole ocean of stories.

Build recurring series so every sailing feels fresh without starting from zero.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Topics become easier when you make a series

A topic and a content pillar

What it is: A topic is what a particular post is about. A content pillar is a broader subject you return to regularly.

Why it matters: A few familiar subjects give you direction without forcing you to invent a completely new identity every week.

Cruise example: “Cabin storage” is a topic. “Practical cruise advice” could be a pillar that includes storage, packing, and getting around the ship.

Your first try: Choose three broad subjects you enjoy explaining: for example, first cruises, no-fly planning, and everyday ship life.

A format and a series

What it is: A format is the way you present an idea: a demonstration, question-and-answer, comparison, or personal story. A series is a group of related posts with a recognizable theme.

Why it matters: Repeating a format makes planning easier, while a series helps viewers know what they can come back for.

Cruise example: “Mariela Answers” could be a weekly series. Each post uses a viewer’s question, a direct answer, and one visual example.

Your first try: Choose one question from your comments and answer it using the same simple structure you can repeat next week.

Now put it into practice

Turn one experience into five useful posts

A cabin becomes a room tour, a storage demonstration, a noise observation, a packing lesson, and an answer to a viewer’s question. Capture each with a different promise; don’t repost the same tour five times.

Keep the receipt of the claim. Record the ship, sailing date, venue, what you paid, what was included, and any special eligibility. Save a private screenshot or source note. Label personal observations as your experience on that sailing.
CHAPTER 07 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

A sailing plan that leaves time to enjoy it.

Use these as filming itineraries. They are examples, not Royal Caribbean schedules or confirmed routes.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

A filming plan is different from a travel itinerary

An itinerary and a shot list

What it is: Your travel itinerary describes where and when you travel. A filming itinerary adds a few planned recording moments. A shot list names the individual views you want to capture.

Why it matters: Separating them keeps the trip’s logistics and safety ahead of the content. A short list also helps you avoid forgetting essential footage.

Cruise example: Travel plan: visit a port and return on time. Shot list: a permitted location view, one activity detail, and a short reflection afterward.

Your first try: Plan only three must-have shots for one day. Add a clear stopping time so you can enjoy the rest of it.

Embarkation, disembarkation, and sea days

What it is: Embarkation means boarding at the start of the cruise. Disembarkation means leaving at the end. A port day includes a destination call; a sea day is spent sailing without that day’s port visit.

Why it matters: Viewers new to cruising may not know these words. Explaining them makes your advice welcoming and prevents confusion about timing.

Cruise example: “Embarkation day—your boarding day—is when I keep my essentials in my carry-on.”

Your first try: The first time you use a cruise term in a beginner video, add its everyday meaning in the same sentence.

Capturing versus posting

What it is: Capturing means recording the material. Posting means publishing it for other people to see. They can happen on different days.

Why it matters: You do not have to edit or publish while trying to enjoy a port. Posting later also lets you verify details and avoid sharing your live location.

Cruise example: Record your port experience, write a note about the price, and make the finished video after returning home.

Your first try: Make a private note right after the experience, then choose a calm editing window later.

Now put it into practice

Before choosing a no-fly cruise

Compare ports you can realistically reach by car, rail, or bus: travel time, parking or transfers, overnight stay, luggage, accessibility, and the journey home. Examples to investigate include Miami, Port Everglades, Port Canaveral, Tampa, Galveston, Baltimore, and Cape Liberty. Ships, routes, seasons, and departure availability vary; check the live booking. Mariela’s home port and actual travel radius are not assumed.

Choose round trips if you need to return to the same land transport. A repositioning cruise may end far away. Allow an arrival buffer for traffic and weather; an overnight stay near port can reduce pressure. No-fly travel still needs a disruption plan: a missed ship or emergency abroad can complicate getting home.

Example: seven-night content itinerary

DayCapture in 20–40 minutesUseful post / logistics
Before departurePacking, redacted planning screen, drive preparationNo-fly checklist; arrange home responsibilities and return transport
EmbarkationPermitted exterior, luggage, first meal, quiet reflectionFirst-hour guide; check in and complete safety requirements before filming
Sea day 1Cabin tour when tidy, storage, one venueCabin decision; write down noise and walking-distance observations
Port day 1Establishing view, route detail, permitted activity, returnPort plan with costs, mobility demands, shade, toilets, and transport
Sea day 2One perk demonstration, food comparisonWho qualifies? What did I actually use?
Port day 2One focused activity with a weather alternativeWas it worth my time? Distinguish ship excursion from independent booking
Last full dayFavorite moment, honest downside, packingWhat I would repeat; check disembarkation instructions
DisembarkationPermitted exterior after completing formalities; home recapActual total cost and next-time lesson; don’t film security or document checks

Three-night version

Day 1: first-hour tip and cabin proof. Day 2: one port or ship experience. Day 3: value comparison and reflection. After: post the recap and answer one recurring question. Aim for four to six strong posts, not nonstop filming.

Embarkation checklist

A port-day shot and safety plan

Before leaving, note ship time versus local time, the posted all-aboard deadline, transport back, emergency contacts, and a substantial return buffer. The port-call deadline is separate from embarkation check-in. Never use a generic “one hour before” rule. Follow the actual ship instructions.

Get one wide location shot, a walking-route detail, a permitted activity close-up, and a reflection. Ask before filming vendors or people. Include currency, transport costs, uneven surfaces, steps, heat, shade, bathrooms, and accessible alternatives when observed. Say “I encountered these steps,” rather than declaring a destination accessible for everyone. Stop filming if weather, wildlife rules, traffic, or a guide requires your attention.

Independent playbook for Mariela Alvarez
CHAPTER 08 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Explain perks without making promises.

POLICY SNAPSHOT · Researched November 2, 2026. These details can change. Recheck official sources before every policy-based post.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

An experience is different from a policy

An observation and a claim

What it is: An observation describes what you personally saw or did. A claim tells viewers something they may rely on as a fact or promise.

Why it matters: Your experience is useful, but one experience cannot prove a rule for every ship, guest, or sailing.

Cruise example: “My room was ready at this time on this sailing” is an observation. “Everyone can enter their room at that time” is a much broader claim.

Your first try: Before publishing, underline each statement someone might use to make a booking or spending decision. Verify those statements.

Eligibility, exclusions, and sources

What it is: Eligibility means who qualifies. Exclusions name what is left out. A source is where the information comes from, ideally the current official policy or booking terms.

Why it matters: A perk can be real and still apply only to certain tiers, cabins, offers, venues, or dates. The limitation is part of the explanation.

Cruise example: A benefit you receive through your loyalty tier may not apply to someone taking their first cruise.

Your first try: For each perk, answer: what is it, who gets it, where does it work, what is excluded, and when did I check?

Evergreen versus changeable information

What it is: Evergreen advice stays useful over time, such as speaking clearly. Changeable information can be updated, such as a fee, package inclusion, or loyalty rule.

Why it matters: An older video can keep circulating after its policy details become outdated. Dating and checking those details helps protect viewer trust.

Cruise example: “Keep private details out of your video” is evergreen advice. A quoted package price belongs to a particular booking and date.

Your first try: Add the ship and sailing month to observations, and record the date you checked any policy you explain.

Now put it into practice

Evergreen: show evidence, name eligibility, and label your personal experience.
Changeable: loyalty benefits, fares, fees, venues, packages, destinations, documents, check-in, and filming permissions. This offline file does not update itself.

Crown & Anchor: a careful starting point

Source: Royal’s loyalty benefits FAQ and program page, checked November 2, 2026. Mariela’s own tier is not known.

The program page describes one point per completed night, with additional earning for qualifying suite and solo bookings. Eligibility and category details matter; consult the program rules. Don’t assume a hosted rate or upgrade earns a particular number of points—confirm the booking terms. New tier benefits apply on a subsequent sailing, not halfway through the trip that earns them.

Source discrepancy: the benefits grid’s general terms contain a 75-point Diamond reference, while the program page and FAQ list 80. Use 80 as the published page threshold and ask Crown & Anchor to resolve conflicting language before advising someone near a threshold. Do not present the inconsistency as a new benefit.

The current benefits grid lists daily drink vouchers for Diamond / Diamond Plus / Pinnacle at 4 / 5 / 6 respectively, with price caps and venue or regional exclusions. Check the footnotes and onboard account before quoting caps or redemption rules. A voucher is not an unlimited beverage package.

Points Choice and status matching are different: the first concerns eligible points allocation; the second concerns recognized tier status. Royal’s program page describes Points Choice for sailings departing January 30, 2026 onward and requests before sailing or within 14 days after disembarkation. Recheck eligibility, exchange rates, and the destination program’s enrollment. Do not say all brands pool lifetime points.

Keep four kinds of perks separate: Crown & Anchor loyalty, casino offers, suite-category benefits, and a creator partnership. Getting a complimentary cruise for content does not create a public loyalty benefit or guarantee another creator the same offer.

The FAQ answer desk

Viewer questionResponsible answer patternVerify here

The 60-second fact check

Document hub guidance varies by departure region. Don’t turn a U.S. closed-loop exception into worldwide advice. A preference not to fly does not remove travel-document requirements. Confirm your own itinerary with Royal and the relevant government authorities.

CHAPTER 09 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Answer the people. Protect your time.

Your comments are a research desk, not an obligation to stay online all day.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Comments are conversations and idea requests

Engagement and community

What it is: Engagement means actions people take around your content, such as asking questions, sharing it, or saving it. Your community is the group of people who return and interact over time.

Why it matters: Useful conversations reveal what viewers need and help them feel heard. The aim is a helpful relationship, not replying to every notification immediately.

Cruise example: Five people asking the same packing question gives you a clear idea for a useful new video.

Your first try: Set one short time to review comments. Save repeated questions in your notes.

Pinned comments, saved replies, and reply videos

What it is: A pinned comment is kept near the top when the platform supports it. A saved reply is wording you reuse and personalize. A reply video answers a comment with a new video.

Why it matters: These tools let one thoughtful answer help many people and reduce repeated typing.

Cruise example: Pin a dated correction so people can find it. Use a reply video when a question needs a visual demonstration.

Your first try: Give a short direct answer when possible; turn the questions needing a demonstration into a future video.

Moderation and boundaries

What it is: Moderation means managing the conversation, including removing private details or abusive material. Boundaries are the limits you set on time, topics, and contact.

Why it matters: Protecting the conversation and your energy makes content creation sustainable. A stranger’s comment is not a demand for instant personal support.

Cruise example: A booking problem belongs with Royal or a travel advisor; a public comment should not contain a reservation number.

Your first try: Write one friendly community rule and choose a daily stopping time for replies.

Now put it into practice

A manageable reply rhythm

Try two 15-minute sessions on posting days, then one short daily check. Pin a helpful question, group duplicates into a future video, and stop when the timer ends. These are workload suggestions, not algorithm requirements. Never sacrifice your port return or vacation to keep replying.

Comment typeBest next stepPossible reply
Quick factual questionShort answer with date/context“On my [ship/date], this was [detail]. Check your sailing’s app because it can vary.”
Repeated questionOne saved answer + a reply video“Several of you asked this. I’m making a walkthrough and will add it to my First Cruise series.”
Personal booking issueRoute to official support“Royal or your travel advisor needs to check your booking. Please don’t post your reservation number here.”
CorrectionVerify, acknowledge, update“Thank you for flagging that. I checked [source/date]; the correct detail is [X]. I’ve updated the caption.”
Different experienceBe curious and specific“That’s helpful context. Which ship and month was that? Mine was [ship/date].”
Rude or harassingModerate instead of arguingHide/report abusive material; block repeated harassment. Leave respectful criticism visible.
Medical, visa or legal issueAvoid personal advice“That depends on your situation. Please confirm with the relevant professional or authority before you travel.”
ComplimentBrief personal connection“That made me smile. I’m glad it helped you plan.”

When a comment becomes a video

Choose a question many travelers can use. Ask permission before prominently featuring a person; otherwise anonymize it and remove profile details. Open with the question, answer it first, show proof, and give the important caveat. Reply under the original comment with the title of the new video. Put evergreen answers in a pinned FAQ or a playlist when the platform supports it.

A community rule you can pin

Welcome aboard! Share your ship and sailing month when it helps the question. Please keep booking numbers, cabin numbers, passports, and personal details private. Experiences vary, and kind corrections are always welcome.

Use saved replies as a starting point, then add one personal sentence. Don’t mass-post identical replies. Don’t ask followers to send private booking details to an unverified account. Add a disclosure when a sponsored reply itself endorses the brand; earlier posts may not be seen by that viewer.

CHAPTER 10 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Free cruise. Clear relationship.

Treat each partnership like a small production: clear terms, honest claims, and a disclosure viewers can understand.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Understand the business words before accepting the work

A sponsorship or hosted experience

What it is: A sponsorship is an arrangement involving a brand and your content. A hosted experience means someone provides some or all of an experience, such as a cruise or dinner, rather than you paying the normal cost yourself.

Why it matters: You need to understand what you are receiving and what work is expected in return. “Free” can still come with substantial production responsibilities.

Cruise example: A cruise offered in exchange for two videos is a work arrangement you should clarify before agreeing.

Your first try: Write down what is covered, what you still pay, and what you are expected to create.

Disclosure and a material connection

What it is: A disclosure is a clear explanation to viewers of your relevant relationship with a brand. A material connection is a relationship or benefit that could affect how viewers judge an endorsement.

Why it matters: Viewers deserve to understand the context of a recommendation. The guidance and examples below explain how to make the actual relationship clear.

Cruise example: A cruise provided in exchange for content is important context even when your opinion is honest.

Your first try: Read the examples below and choose wording that describes exactly what was provided. Never copy a disclosure that is not true for your arrangement.

Deliverables, approvals, and revisions

What it is: Deliverables are the specific things you promise to provide. Approval is a required review before delivery or posting. Revisions are requested changes to your work.

Why it matters: A vague promise to “make content” can create different expectations about how many videos, how much work, and when it is due.

Cruise example: Two vertical videos and ten photos by an agreed date are clearer than “some cruise posts.”

Your first try: List the number, format, length expectations, deadlines, review process, and included rounds of changes.

Usage rights, paid ads, and exclusivity

What it is: Usage rights describe where and for how long another party may use your work. Paid ads are placements a brand pays to show. Exclusivity limits work you may do with other brands.

Why it matters: Letting a brand repost a video can be different from letting it run the video as an advertisement or restrict future work. These terms affect the agreement’s value and scope.

Cruise example: A brand might ask to repost your video for a month, use it in ads, or run ads through your account. Each request needs clear agreed terms.

Your first try: Ask what uses are included, for how long, on which channels, and whether further permission or payment is required. Review unfamiliar terms before agreeing.

Affiliate links, media kits, and campaign reports

What it is: An affiliate link can earn you a commission from qualifying activity. A media kit introduces your audience, work, and services. A campaign report summarizes what you delivered and the measured results.

Why it matters: These are separate tools for earning, pitching, and reporting. You can build them gradually as your content develops.

Cruise example: A simple media kit could show your story, three representative videos, audience information you actually have, and your contact details.

Your first try: Keep your best examples and a record of real results. Do not invent audience figures or guaranteed bookings.

Now put it into practice

FTC guidance, checked November 2, 2026: free or discounted travel and other valuable perks can create a material connection. A truthful opinion still needs an appropriate disclosure. Use the exact relationship, not vague “thanks,” “collab,” or “ambassador” alone. FTC Disclosures 101.

Disclosure examples to adapt truthfully

Hosted cruise

“Royal Caribbean provided this cruise at no charge in exchange for content.” Say it and show readable text near the beginning. Put the relationship at the start of the caption too.

Paid + hosted

“Ad: Royal Caribbean paid me and provided this cruise to create this video.” Use only if both are true.

Specific gifted perk

“Royal Caribbean provided this specialty dinner for free.” Describe the actual benefit; don’t imply the whole trip was hosted.

Affiliate relationship

“I earn a commission if you book through this link.” Put the explanation beside the link and in the endorsement where needed.

Put the disclosure where the endorsement happens

For video, include it in the video; audio plus visible text improves notice. For a Story, place readable text on the endorsing frame. Repeat periodically during a live stream. Use platform paid-partnership tools in addition to your own clear wording. A profile note, buried hashtag, or caption hidden behind “more” is easy to miss. Match the language of the content, including translated disclosures for other languages. FTC guide.

Disclose each relevant post separately. Promoting Royal during a hosted trip needs the relationship explained; an unrelated shop you independently visited does not automatically have a connection to you. Explain any actual shop relationship. Only describe experiences you had and claims you can support; don’t accept a script requiring a false opinion. FTC endorsement Q&A, including its free-cruise example.

Agree on the work before you board

Permission to create is part of the brief

Royal publishes production filming guidelines covering approved representatives, guest privacy, safety and location restrictions. They are not blanket authorization for a creator. Get your partnership contact’s current written filming plan. Do not film security screening, document checks, safety drills, or restricted areas. Ask before filming crew or identifiable guests; get parent/guardian authorization for children and follow the production’s release requirements. Avoid show footage unless specifically cleared.

Royal’s guest conduct policy prohibits drone operation onboard, near the vessel, at private destinations and in port facilities; personal-drone carriage is not commercial filming permission. Do not plan drone content without explicit brand/location approval and applicable legal permissions. Respect crew instructions, local rules, music rights and privacy. Never publish barcodes, boarding passes, cabin numbers, minors’ locations or private conversations.

Independent playbook for Mariela Alvarez
CHAPTER 11 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

From idea to posted—with breathing room.

A monthly sailing can support a month of useful content. Plan a modest output you can deliver comfortably.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

A workflow makes the job repeatable

Pre-production, production, and post-production

What it is: Pre-production is preparation. Production is recording. Post-production is the work after recording, including editing and checks. A workflow is the repeatable order of these tasks.

Why it matters: A clear order reduces last-minute decisions and helps you know what “finished” means.

Cruise example: Plan a cabin tip before boarding, record it in the cabin, then edit and check the details afterward.

Your first try: Use three headings in your notes: before filming, while filming, and after filming.

Batching and a content calendar

What it is: Batching means doing similar tasks together. A content calendar is a simple plan for what you will post and when.

Why it matters: You can record several short explanations in one quiet session instead of setting up your phone each time. A calendar spreads the work out.

Cruise example: Record three introductions in your cabin, then collect the matching detail shots at appropriate times. Publish them on different days.

Your first try: Plan just the next two posts. Set aside a short recording window and a separate editing window.

A backup and a clean master

What it is: A backup is an extra copy stored separately. A clean master is your finished video saved without a platform watermark, with the elements you intend to keep.

Why it matters: Phones can run out of space or fail. Keeping originals and finished copies helps you recover work and make later corrections.

Cruise example: Your phone holds the original clips; a second secure location holds a backup. An Exports folder holds finished videos.

Your first try: Create separate folders for original clips and finished videos, and make a second copy when practical.

Now put it into practice

01 / PLAN

7–14 days before

Choose three audience questions and one story. Review sponsorship scope, claims, permissions and sources. Make a shot list. Prepare hooks and three-word cues, not pages of prose.

02 / CAPTURE

During the sailing

Use one short morning and one optional afternoon filming window. Record the must-have proof first. Log venue/date/cost details while fresh; keep private notes separate from public captions.

03 / ASSEMBLE

Each evening, 15 minutes

Favorite the useful clips, rename or organize them by day/topic, and back up when practical. Draft one takeaway. Avoid uploading large files over an insecure or expensive connection without checking the plan.

04 / PUBLISH

When ready

Check facts, edit, caption, disclose, and preview. Get required contractual review. Post after leaving a location if live location is unnecessary. Save the final caption and published URL.

05 / LEARN

7 and 30 days later

Capture metrics at consistent ages. Send the agreed brand report. Compare to your own similar posts. Let repeated questions shape the next sailing.

Four-week publishing rhythm

WeekSuggested postsProduction focus
Before sailingPacking tip + no-fly planning answerPrepare evergreen tips before departure
Sailing weekFirst impression + one useful demonstrationCapture proof; post only when practical
Week afterCabin/ship lesson + value comparisonEdit from verified notes and receipts
Before next sailingComment reply + personal reflectionReview results, refresh facts, prepare next brief

Two posts a week is a starting workload, not a growth guarantee. A sponsored agreement may require different deliverables. Build rest days into the plan.

File habits that save the next edit

Use folders like 2026-11_ShipName / Originals / Audio / Exports / Sources / Reports. Name useful clips D02_Cabin_Storage_Close_01. Keep original files until delivery and any agreed retention period end. Back up to a second secure location when possible. Separate guest releases and contracts from clips you share publicly.

The publishing gate

Your pocket planning studio.

Build a short script, save your notes, and take your plan with you. Everything here runs in this file.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

How to use the planning tools below

A video brief and an outline

What it is: A brief is a short description of what you want to make and who it helps. An outline puts the ideas in order without requiring a word-for-word speech.

Why it matters: These tools help you choose the point before filming and keep the explanation manageable.

Cruise example: Topic: carry-on essentials. Audience: first-time cruiser. Proof: your bag and three items. Limit: room access timing varies.

Your first try: Fill in those four fields, choose the actual brand relationship, and press “Create my outline.” Replace every bracket with a true detail.

Exporting and importing notes

What it is: Exporting makes a downloadable backup of your notes. Importing loads a previous backup into this playbook. The notes file uses a format called JSON; you do not need to read or edit its code.

Why it matters: Browser saving may not travel with the HTML file to another device. A separate notes backup helps you take your planning with you.

Cruise example: Export your notes on your computer, then import that notes file when using this playbook on another supported device.

Your first try: After writing a useful plan, use “Export my notes.” Keep that backup with your playbook file.

Now put it into practice

Your checklists and notes save in this browser when local storage is available. Local-file behavior varies by browser. Use Export my notes for a portable backup. This file sends no data anywhere. Do not enter private booking, passport, or medical information.

Build a video brief

Your editable outline

This creates a planning scaffold, not verified cruise facts. Replace prompts with your actual observations.

Eyeline practice card

Ready. Your notes stay on this device.

Place this window close to the camera lens. Read, look at the lens, then speak.

CHAPTER 13 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Templates you can make your own.

Useful starting points for real experiences. Replace the brackets, check the facts, and speak naturally.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Templates are starting points for your own words

A template and a placeholder

What it is: A template is a reusable structure. A placeholder is a prompt you replace, such as [ship] or [actual price].

Why it matters: A structure makes writing less intimidating, but leaving the prompts in place or guessing details makes the result confusing or inaccurate.

Cruise example: Replace “[ship / sailing date]” with your actual ship and month, and replace “[proof]” with what you personally recorded.

Your first try: Open one template, copy it, and replace every bracket. Then read it aloud and simplify anything you would not naturally say.

Adapting a template for speech

What it is: Written wording often needs to become shorter and more conversational when spoken. An outline can guide you without becoming something you read stiffly.

Why it matters: Viewers connect more easily with a clear explanation in your own voice than with a long paragraph delivered word for word.

Cruise example: “Here is the storage I used” can sound more natural than a formal introduction to your cabin review.

Your first try: Read your completed draft once, turn it into three cue words, and explain it to the lens in short takes.

Now put it into practice

30-second FAQ answer
[Disclosure if relevant.] You asked: [question]. On [ship] in [month/year], my experience was [direct answer]. Here’s what I saw: [proof]. The important limit is [eligibility/exclusion]. Check [official source or your sailing app] before you plan. Save this for [specific use].
Honest perk explanation
[Disclosure.] I received [perk] because of [tier, cabin, offer, or creator agreement]. It helped me [actual result]. It does not mean every guest gets it. Check [current source] for [eligibility and limits]. My personal takeaway: [who it might help].
Cabin review
[Disclosure.] This is [ship / cabin category / sailing date]. I’ll show you [three useful things]. What worked for me: [specifics]. What I’d consider before booking again: [noise, space, location or tradeoff]. This is one cabin on one sailing; verify your exact category and deck plan.
Port-day story
[Disclosure if relevant.] We had [actual time available] in [port]. I chose [activity] because [reason]. It cost me [dated amount / currency / inclusions]. Here’s the route and what I encountered: [transport, steps, shade, restrooms]. I returned with [actual buffer]. Check your own all-aboard time and conditions.
Value comparison
[Disclosure.] For my [ship/date] booking, option A cost [total incl. applicable additions], and option B cost [comparable total]. I used [actual amount]. For my habits, [conclusion]. Your quote and usage may differ; compare [specific terms] before buying.
Personal no-fly story
I prefer not to fly, so I planned [land journey] to [port]. The part I prepared for was [traffic, luggage, overnight or return journey]. What helped was [real lesson]. Next time I’d [change]. If you travel this way too, what is your biggest planning question?
A correction that builds trust
Correction to my [date/topic] post: I said [old claim]. The current official source says [correct claim] for [scope]. I checked it on [date] and updated [caption/pinned comment/replacement video]. Thank you to the viewers who flagged this.
Caption + source note
[Clear relationship disclosure if relevant.] [Specific takeaway in one sentence.] Ship: [name] • Sailed: [month/year] • Eligibility: [scope]. My experience: [observation]. Prices/perks may vary. Policy source: [official URL], checked [date]. [One useful question or action.]
Brand delivery report
Campaign: [name] • Sailing: [ship/date] • Reporting window: [dates]. Delivered: [URLs / formats / disclosure status]. Results at [7 or 30] days: [reach, views, watch time, saves, shares, clicks with definitions]. Audience questions: [top themes]. What worked: [evidence]. Next test: [one change]. Costs/compensation and usage rights: [as agreed, in private report].
CHAPTER 14 · MARIELA’S CREATOR PLAYBOOK

Measure usefulness, not just views.

Learn what the performance numbers mean, why they matter, and how to use them to make one small improvement.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Understand the numbers before judging your videos

Analytics, metrics, and KPIs

What it is: Analytics is the information a platform gives you about how your content performs. A metric is one measurement. A KPI, or key performance indicator, is a measurement you choose because it relates to your goal.

Why it matters: A large number is not automatically the right sign of success. A useful packing guide may matter because people save it, not because it reaches the most people.

Cruise example: If your goal is helping people prepare, saves and practical questions may be useful KPIs. If a brand asks for link visits, measured clicks may matter too.

Your first try: Choose one goal and two numbers connected to it. Start with the information your platform already provides.

Views, reach, and impressions

What it is: Views count viewing events using the platform’s rules. Reach generally describes the distinct accounts shown the content. Impressions count displays and can include repeat exposure to the same account.

Why it matters: These numbers describe different things. One person can see or watch a post more than once, so views are not always the number of people reached.

Cruise example: A video may have more views than accounts reached because some people watched again.

Your first try: Write down the exact label and definition shown in your platform instead of treating views and people as interchangeable.

Watch time, retention, and completion

What it is: Watch time is time spent watching. Average watch time is the average per measured view. Retention describes how viewing continues or drops during the video. Completion measures reaching the end under the platform’s definition.

Why it matters: These help you spot where an explanation holds attention or becomes confusing. They measure different things and are not a verdict on your personality.

Cruise example: If viewers leave during a long greeting, test an opening that shows the useful result earlier.

Your first try: Look at one video’s viewing pattern. Find one place to clarify or shorten, rather than changing everything at once.

Rates and denominators

What it is: A rate puts a count in relation to another number. The denominator is the number you divide by. Multiply the result by 100 to express it as a percentage.

Why it matters: Twenty-five saves mean something different when 100 people were reached than when 10,000 were reached. Using a consistent denominator makes comparisons clearer.

Cruise example: 25 saves ÷ 1,000 accounts reached × 100 = a 2.5% save rate. 18 average seconds ÷ a 30-second video × 100 = a 60% watch ratio; that is not a completion rate.

Your first try: Use the calculator below with example numbers first. Compare the same rate, using the same denominator, across similar posts.

A baseline, median, and a test

What it is: A baseline is your starting result. The median is the middle result when numbers are sorted. A test changes one thing so you can learn whether it seems to help.

Why it matters: Comparing with your own usual results is more useful than chasing another creator’s best-performing post. A small sample can still be noisy.

Cruise example: Sort five save rates: 1%, 2%, 3%, 4%, 10%. The median is 3%. Try a clearer hook in several similar videos and compare later results.

Your first try: Collect results from your first few similar videos before setting an improvement goal. Treat a single unusually good or bad post as one observation.

Now put it into practice

MeasureHow to read itWhat to try next
Early retentionUse the platform’s first-seconds or retention curve when available. Note the exact definition.Large early drop? Show the result sooner and remove the preamble.
Average watch timeSeconds watched on average; compare with length. Replays may affect it.Drop at a confusing explanation? Shorten or demonstrate that step.
Completion rateUse the platform’s completed-view definition consistently.Test a clearer structure on videos of similar duration.
Save / share rateSaves or shares ÷ reach × 100, using the same denominator each time.More saves on practical checklists? Make another specific checklist.
Helpful commentsCount substantive questions, reports of usefulness and misconceptions.A recurring question can become the next post.
Profile / link actionTrack profile visits, follows or link clicks with available analytics.Check whether your promise matches your profile and linked offer.
Partner outcomesUse agreed tracked links or codes, with permission and clear attribution.Report attributed actions honestly; clicks alone do not prove bookings.

A small measurement tool

Example inputs only. Average watch ÷ duration is a watch ratio, not completion rate. Replays can take it over 100%. Reach and views are different measures.

Your first 30-day experiment

  1. Publish a manageable set of 6–8 useful videos. Capture results at day 7 and day 30.
  2. Group comparable videos by length and format. Find your median watch ratio and save rate.
  3. Choose one test: a demonstration-first opening versus a question-first opening. Keep topic and length as similar as practical.
  4. Use several posts per approach. Small samples and changing audiences limit conclusions.
  5. Keep the version that helps your audience and is sustainable to make.

There is no universal “good” retention rate. Set an initial goal against your own baseline, such as improving median save rate over the next month, and write down the sample size. Report reach, views and clicks with their platform definitions. Don’t buy engagement or promise a brand a booking count you cannot substantiate.

LEARN IT FIRST · THEN TRY IT

Use the sources as your reference shelf

An official source and an access date

What it is: An official source is published by the organization responsible for the information, such as Royal Caribbean for its program rules or the FTC for its guidance. The access date records when you checked it.

Why it matters: Policies and guidance may change after a video or this playbook was created. Keeping the source and date helps you revisit the actual wording.

Cruise example: A remembered benefit from an old cruise can be checked against the current benefits grid and your sailing’s terms.

Your first try: Open the relevant link before a policy-heavy post. Read the conditions, and ask the responsible organization if sources conflict.

Refresh before publishing

Revisit relevant official sources before each sailing and each policy-heavy post. Save a dated private note; update your public caption or pin a correction if an old claim becomes misleading.
